lines: Dry rows and trampled crops teach a farmer to watch every footstep.
The soil's been kind lately. That's more than I can say for some visitors.
Seeds are small, but they know how to make a person <pulse>wait</pulse>.
Good rain is a blessing. Too much rain is work wearing a blessing mask.
A harvest is just a hundred small chores deciding to agree.
Bread starts long before the oven. Most good things do.
Most days, I am at the fields, trying to keep rain and soil from becoming everyone else's problem.
People think crops is simple until something goes wrong and suddenly it is very important.
A village runs on small work. Nobody praises it until it stops happening.
I trust a good hoe more than a loud promise. The hoe has less to prove.
You remember that walk through {follow_biome}? I have tilled softer ground than that road.
I remember following you through {follow_biome}. My feet remember it even better.
That trip across {follow_biome} taught me to ask more questions before walking.
Following you taught me that plans sound much safer before anyone starts walking.
I kept up, mostly. My feet have a harsher opinion of the trip.
Next time, warn me before the road becomes a test of character.
I learned two things out there: stay close, and ask better questions earlier.
You move like danger is a normal part of the route. I am still adjusting to that.
It was not all bad. Some views are worth sore legs and nervous glances.
If I followed you again, I would pack more food and fewer assumptions.
Boats are not much like fields. No furrows, no rows, just water deciding if it likes you.
That boat trip still sits oddly in my memory, but at least it floated.
A boat can make a bad plan quieter. It can't make me forget it.

I notice the little things. That is either a skill or what the fields has done to me.
